items.followUp: Define empirical formula and give one example.

rubric.why: The definition must identify the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it shows the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule.

rubric.why: A correct chemical formula demonstrates the definition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct molecular formula.

modelAnswer: A molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms of each element present in one molecule of a substance.
For example, the molecular formula of water is H₂O.

items.followUp: Define an ion and state how it is formed from an atom.

accept: equal number of protons and electrons
rubric.why: An atom has no overall charge because its positive and negative charges balance.
rubric.description: States that an atom is neutral.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that an atom has no net charge or has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

rubric.why: An ion is formed when an atom gains or loses electrons, giving it a net charge.
rubric.description: Distinguishes an ion from an atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an ion is charged, or that it forms by electron gain or loss.

modelAnswer: An atom is electrically neutral because it has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
An ion is a charged particle formed when an atom gains or loses electrons.

items.followUp: What is nuclear fission, and how can it be used to generate electricity?

rubric.why: Uranium-235 releases energy when its nucleus undergoes fission; in a reactor the reaction is controlled.
rubric.description: Identifies fission of U-235 as the energy source.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that U-235 undergoes fission, preferably as a controlled chain reaction.

rubric.why: The heat released is used to produce steam, which drives a turbine connected to a generator.
rubric.description: Explains how the released energy generates electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the heat to steam driving a turbine or generator.

modelAnswer: Uranium-235 undergoes a controlled nuclear fission chain reaction in a reactor, releasing heat.
The heat produces steam, which turns a turbine connected to an electric generator.

items.followUp: State one major limitation of Rutherford’s atomic model.

rubric.why: According to classical physics, revolving electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus, so the model could not explain atomic stability.
rubric.description: Explains that Rutherford’s model could not account for atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it could not explain why electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus.

rubric.why: The model did not explain the discrete line spectra of atoms.
rubric.description: Identifies the failure to explain atomic spectra.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the model could not explain the line spectra of atoms.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability: revolving electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus.
It also could not explain the line spectra of atoms.

items.followUp: Why does atomic radius generally decrease from left to right across a period?

rubric.why: Across a period, proton number and nuclear charge increase.
rubric.description: States that nuclear charge increases across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the increasing nuclear charge.

rubric.why: The stronger attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons raises the energy needed to remove an electron.
rubric.description: Links stronger attraction to increasing ionization energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the outer electron is held more strongly (with a smaller atomic radius as supporting detail).

modelAnswer: Across a period, nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell.
The stronger attraction holds the outer electrons more firmly, so more energy is needed to remove one.

items.followUp: Why are elements in Groups 1 and 17 called s-block and p-block elements, respectively?

rubric.why: The block name depends on the subshell into which the last electron enters.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the last electron enters an s subshell for s-block elements.

rubric.why: The block name depends on the subshell into which the last electron enters.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the last electron enters a p subshell for p-block elements.

modelAnswer: They are called s-block elements because the last electron enters an s subshell.
They are called p-block elements because the last electron enters a p subshell.

items.followUp: What is the modern periodic law, and on what basis did Moseley arrange the elements?

rubric.why: Moseley established atomic number as the correct basis for arranging elements.
rubric.description: Identifies atomic number as the basis of Moseley’s arrangement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Moseley arranged elements by increasing atomic number, not atomic mass.

rubric.why: Moseley’s work led to the modern periodic law relating periodic properties to atomic number.
rubric.description: States the contribution to the periodic law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that elemental properties recur periodically when elements are arranged by atomic number.

modelAnswer: Moseley showed that elements should be arranged in order of increasing atomic number, rather than atomic mass.
His work established the modern periodic law: the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

items.followUp: Name the two ways atoms can achieve a stable outer shell by bonding.

rubric.why: An atom can achieve an octet by gaining or losing electrons through transfer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that atoms gain or lose electrons (electron transfer).

rubric.why: Atoms can also achieve an octet by sharing electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that atoms share electrons.

modelAnswer: An atom can attain eight electrons in its valence shell by gaining or losing electrons (electron transfer).
It can also attain an octet by sharing electrons with another atom.
